a1-06.explain: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun that matches the subject: me levanto (I get up), te sientas (you sit), se sienta (he/she sits), se sientan (they sit). It goes before the verb: llamarse, sentarse, casarse, reírse. Watch out: English often has no 'myself' here, but Spanish needs the pronoun: 'Kiara se casa' = Kiara is getting married.
examples: El tío Wilfredo no se sienta con su hermano Héctor.
Uncle Wilfredo won't sit with his brother Héctor.
¡Qué problema! Me levanto a las cinco para pensar.
What a problem! I get up at five to think about it.
El sábado, los hermanos pierden... y se ríen juntos.
On Saturday, the brothers lose... and laugh together.

a1-06.explain: For 'I', regular present verbs end in -o: preparar → preparo, vivir → vivo, levantarse → me levanto. Because the -o already shows 'I', Spanish usually leaves out 'yo' (use it for emphasis or contrast). Watch out: some very common verbs are irregular in the yo form: soy, estoy, voy, tengo.
examples: Me llamo Yadira y vivo en San Juan.
My name is Yadira and I live in San Juan.
Yo preparo las mesas de la boda.
I'm doing the seating plan for the wedding.
— ¡Tengo hambre y me gusta mucho el bizcocho!
"I'm hungry, and I really like cake!"

a1-06.explain: Possessives go before the noun: mi = my, su = his, her or their (also formal 'your'). Spanish has no apostrophe-s, so 'Kiara's mother-in-law' is la suegra de Kiara. Watch out: su can mean his, her or their, so the story tells you who; and before a plural noun add -s: mis primos, sus hermanos.
examples: Mi prima Kiara se casa el sábado.
My cousin Kiara is getting married on Saturday.
El tío Wilfredo no se sienta con su hermano Héctor.
Uncle Wilfredo won't sit with his brother Héctor.
Mi cuñado Ismael quiere la mesa al lado del bizcocho de fresa.
My brother-in-law Ismael wants the table next to the strawberry cake.

a1-07.explain: 'Hay' (there is / there are) says that something exists, often something new: hay una vista perfecta, hay muchas nubes. It never changes for plural. Watch out: for a specific thing we already know, use estar: Delante está la ciudad (not 'hay la ciudad'). 'Hay sol' means 'it's sunny'.
examples: —Arriba hay una vista perfecta —lee él.
"At the top there is a perfect view," he reads.
—Muchas mañanas hay nubes, pero al mediodía hay sol.
"On a lot of mornings there are clouds, but at midday the sun comes out."
Delante está la ciudad, entre montañas verdes.
The city is right in front of them, among green mountains.

a1-07.explain: 'Se' before a verb marks a reflexive verb in the he/she form: se sienta (sits down), se llama (is called), se levanta (gets up). With 'yo' it is 'me': me siento, me llamo. Watch out: 'la llama sienta' is wrong; you need 'se'. And enjoy the joke: la llama se llama Pelusa!
examples: La llama se sienta en el centro y no se mueve.
The llama sits down in the middle and won't move.
—Se llama Pelusa y vive aquí —dice Killa.
"Her name is Pelusa, and she lives here," says Killa.
A las doce, Pelusa se levanta.
At twelve o'clock, Pelusa gets up.

a1-07.explain: 'Muy' (very) goes before an adjective and never changes: muy vieja, muy triste. 'Mucho' (a lot of, many) goes before a noun and agrees with it: mucho sol, mucha agua, muchos libros, muchas nubes. Watch out: don't say 'mucho triste' for 'very sad'; with adjectives it is always muy.
examples: Pero hoy hay muchas nubes. Marina está muy triste.
But today there are lots of clouds. Marina is very sad.
—Esta es una ciudad inca del siglo quince. ¡Es muy vieja! —dice Killa.
"This is an Inca city from the fifteenth century. It's very old!" says Killa.
—Muchas mañanas hay nubes, pero al mediodía hay sol.
"On a lot of mornings there are clouds, but at midday the sun comes out."

a1-08.explain: 'Tener que' + infinitive means 'have to': tenemos que ir (we have to go). Only tener changes: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, tenemos que, tienen que. Watch out: don't drop 'que' ('tenemos ir' is wrong), and keep the second verb in the infinitive. 'Hay que' + infinitive is the impersonal form, for 'you/we have to' in general: ¡Hay que empezar allí! It never changes.
examples: —¡Tenemos que ir! —dice Julián.
"We have to go!" says Julián.
Van al enorme castillo de San Felipe. ¡Hay que empezar allí!
They go to the huge San Felipe castle. They have to start there!
Mañana tienen que buscar otro libro de piratas.
Tomorrow they have to look for another pirate book.

a1-08.explain: To compare, use 'más + adjective + que' = 'more … than' or '-er than': más dulce que (sweeter than), más pequeño que (smaller than). The adjective agrees with the noun. For 'better', say 'mejor que'; for 'as … as', say 'tan … como'. Watch out: use 'que', not 'de' or 'como', after más (only before a number is it 'más de': más de diez).
examples: El mapa dice: «Castillo. Torre del Reloj. El tesoro es más dulce que el oro».
The map says: "Castle. Clock Tower. The treasure is sweeter than gold."
Un puesto, más pequeño que los otros, tiene un dibujo: ¡una X y un coco!
One stall, smaller than the others, has a drawing: an X and a coconut!
—¡Este tesoro es mejor que el oro! —dice Julián.
"This treasure is better than gold!" says Julián.
Les da dos cocadas tan grandes como sus manos.
She gives them two cocadas as big as their hands.

a1-08.explain: Spanish uses 'tener' for age: Lina tiene once años = Lina is eleven (literally 'has eleven years'). Ask: ¿Cuántos años tienes? Tener also means to have or own: mi hermano tiene la librería. Watch out: never use ser or estar for age ('Lina es once años' is wrong).
examples: Lina tiene once años y su primo Julián tiene nueve.
Lina is eleven and her cousin Julián is nine.
—Porque mi hermano tiene la librería y yo tengo el tesoro.
"Because my brother has the bookshop and I have the treasure."
—¿Tienen el mapa? —pregunta la señora del puesto.
"Do you have the map?" asks the woman at the stall.

a1-08.explain: '¿Por qué?' (two words, with an accent) asks 'why?'. 'Porque' (one word, no accent) answers 'because'. Watch out: they sound almost the same, so the difference shows in writing: question = ¿por qué?, answer = porque.
examples: —¿Por qué es tan grande? —pregunta Julián.
"Why is it so big?" asks Julián.
—Porque los piratas quieren oro, y el castillo es más fuerte que ellos.
"Because pirates want gold, and the castle is stronger than they are."
—Sí. ¿Por qué? —pregunta Lina.
"Yes. Why?" asks Lina.

a1-09.topic: Ir a + infinitive: the near future
a1-09.explain: 'Ir a' + infinitive talks about the future, like English 'going to': voy a cocinar, vas a hacer, va a estar. Pattern: voy/vas/va/vamos/van + a + infinitive. Watch out: don't drop the 'a' ('vas hacer' is wrong), and don't conjugate the second verb ('vas a haces' is wrong).
examples: —Este fin de semana no tengo planes y voy a estar sola.
"This weekend I have no plans and I'm going to be alone."
—Entonces, ¿qué vas a hacer el sábado?
"So, what are you going to do on Saturday?"
—Voy a cocinar una tortilla y ver una película.
"I'm going to cook a tortilla and watch a movie."

a1-09.explain: Question words carry a written accent: ¿qué? (what), ¿por qué? (why), ¿dónde? (where), ¿cómo? (how), ¿cuándo? (when), ¿quién? (who). Written questions open with ¿ and close with ?. '¿Qué tal estás?' = How are you? Watch out: '¿Qué dices?' literally asks 'What are you saying?', but often shows surprise, like 'What?!'
examples: —¡Hola, Marta! ¿Qué tal estás?
"Hi, Marta! How are you?"
—¿Por qué estás triste? —pregunta él.
"Why are you sad?" he asks.
—¿Qué dices? ¡Tú vives en Madrid!
"What are you saying? You live in Madrid!"

a1-09.explain: 'Este' and 'esta' mean 'this'; 'estos' and 'estas' mean 'these'. They agree with the noun: este sábado, esta tarde, estas flores. 'Este fin de semana' = this (coming) weekend. Watch out: 'esta' (this) has no accent, but 'está' (is) does: Esta flor está aquí.
examples: —Este fin de semana no tengo planes y voy a estar sola.
"This weekend I have no plans and I'm going to be alone."
—¡Sorpresa! Estas flores son para ti. Voy a pasar el fin de semana aquí —dice.
"Surprise! These flowers are for you. I'm going to spend the weekend here," he says.
Este sábado no va a estar sola.
This Saturday she is not going to be alone.

a1-10.explain: 'El sábado' = on Saturday; 'a las ocho' = at eight. With a clock time, use 'de la mañana / de la tarde / de la noche': a las ocho de la mañana. Without a clock time, use 'por la mañana / por la tarde / por la noche': el viernes por la noche. Watch out: no 'en' before days.
examples: —A Cádiz. El tren sale a las ocho de la mañana.
"To Cádiz. The train leaves at eight in the morning."
El viernes por la noche, los hermanos preparan las mochilas.
On Friday night, the siblings pack their backpacks.
El sábado, los tres llegan a la estación temprano.
On Saturday, the three of them arrive at the station early.

a1-10.explain: Possessives go before the noun: mi (my), tu (your), su (his, her, their, or formal your). They agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so add -s before a plural noun: mis recuerdos (my memories). Watch out: su can mean his, her or their, so the context tells you who; tu (your) has no accent, tú (you) does.
examples: Elena y su hermano Raúl están en la cocina.
Elena and her brother Raúl are in the kitchen.
Elena se ríe y abre su bolsa.
Elena laughs and opens her bag.
—Es más grande que en mis recuerdos —dice.
"It's bigger than I remember (literally: than in my memories)," he says.

a1-10.explain: Some verbs change the vowel in their stem when it is stressed: querer → quiero, quieres, quiere, quieren (e → ie); encontrar → encuentro, encuentras, encuentra, encuentran (o → ue). The endings stay regular. Watch out: with nosotros the stem does not change: queremos, encontramos.
examples: —Perfecto. Él tiene ochenta años y quiere ver el mar.
"Perfect. He is eighty years old and wants to see the sea."
—Abuelo, ¿quieres ir con nosotros? —pregunta Elena por teléfono.
"Grandpa, do you want to come with us?" Elena asks on the phone.
Raúl busca los billetes, pero no los encuentra.
Raúl looks for the tickets, but he cannot find them.

a1-06.q: Which sentence means 'Uncle Wilfredo doesn't sit with his brother'?
options: El tío Wilfredo no sienta se con su hermano.
El tío Wilfredo se no sienta con su hermano.
El tío Wilfredo no se sienta con su hermano.
El tío Wilfredo no me sienta con su hermano.
a1-06.why: 'No' comes first, then the pronoun, then the verb: no se sienta. With he/she the pronoun is 'se', not 'me'.

a1-06.q: Fill in the blank: Yo ___ las mesas de la boda.
a1-06.why: With 'yo', regular verbs end in -o: preparo. 'Prepara' is he/she, 'preparas' is you, and 'preparar' is the infinitive.

a1-06.q: Complete: El tío Wilfredo no se sienta con ___ hermano Héctor. (his brother)
a1-06.why: 'Su' means his (also her or their). 'Hermano' is singular, so su, not sus. 'Mi' is my and 'tu' is your.

a1-06.q: Complete: Kiara y Joel ___ el sábado.
a1-06.why: Two people = they, so the verb ends in -an and the pronoun is 'se': se casan. The pronoun goes before the verb.
Spanish says 'I have hunger': tengo hambre. Tener is irregular in the yo form (tengo); 'tiene' is he/she, and ser is not used here.

a1-06.q: What does 'Mi prima Kiara se casa el sábado' mean?
options: My cousin Kiara is getting married on Saturday.
His cousin Kiara is getting married on Saturday.
Your cousin Kiara is getting married on Saturday.
Her cousin Kiara gets married every Saturday.
a1-06.why: 'Mi' = my. 'His/her' would be 'su', and 'your' would be 'tu'.

a1-06.q: Yadira talks about her two cousins. Complete: ___ primos se sientan juntos. (My cousins)
a1-06.why: Possessives agree with the thing owned: 'primos' is plural, so mi becomes mis. 'Su/sus' would mean his, her or their.

a1-06.q: Complete: ¡Qué problema! ___ a las cinco para pensar. (I get up)
a1-06.why: Levantarse is reflexive. With 'I' the pronoun is 'me' and the verb ends in -o: me levanto. 'Se levanta' is he/she; 'levanto' alone means 'I lift'.

a1-07.q: Which sentence means 'There are a lot of clouds'?
a1-07.why: 'Hay' introduces things that exist and never changes for plural. 'Mucha nubes' is wrong because 'muchas' must agree with 'nubes'.

a1-07.q: What does 'A las doce, Pelusa se levanta' mean?
a1-07.why: 'Levantarse' is reflexive: she lifts herself up, so she gets up. 'Se sienta' is 'sits down'; 'levantar' without 'se' means to lift something.
Before an adjective (triste) use 'muy', which never changes. 'Mucho/mucha' go before nouns.
Before a noun use mucho, and it agrees with the noun: 'mañanas' is feminine plural, so muchas.

a1-07.q: Complete: Delante ___ la ciudad, entre montañas verdes.
a1-07.why: 'La ciudad' is a specific, known place, so use estar for its location. 'Hay' only introduces something new: hay una ciudad.

a1-07.q: Killa introduces herself. Complete: Hola, ___ Killa.
a1-07.why: Llamarse is reflexive: me llamo (my name is). 'Se llama' is for he/she; 'llamo' alone means 'I call'.

a1-07.q: What does Killa mean with '¡Es muy vieja!'?
a1-07.why: 'Muy' + adjective = very + adjective: muy vieja = very old. 'Vieja' agrees with 'la ciudad'.

a1-07.q: How does the story say 'The sun is out!' (literally 'There is sun')?
a1-07.why: 'Hay sol' (there is sun) is the normal way to say it's sunny. 'Hay' never changes.

a1-09.topic: Ir a + infinitive: the near future
a1-09.q: Which sentence means 'What are you going to do on Saturday?'
a1-09.why: Ir + a + infinitive: vas a hacer. Don't drop 'a', and don't conjugate the second verb.

a1-09.q: Marta answers: 'Estoy bien, pero un poco triste.' What did Javier ask?
a1-09.why: '¿Qué tal estás?' (How are you?) asks how someone is, so 'Estoy bien' answers it. ¿Dónde? asks where; ¿Quién? asks who.

a1-09.q: Complete: —¡Sorpresa! ___ flores son para ti. (These flowers)
a1-09.why: 'Flores' is feminine plural, so 'these' is estas. Este/esta are singular; estos is for masculine nouns.

a1-09.q: Which sentence means 'This weekend I have no plans'?
options: Este fin de semana no tengo planes.
Esta fin de semana no tengo planes.
Estos fin de semana no tengo planes.
Esto fin de semana no tengo planes.
a1-09.why: 'Fin de semana' is masculine singular (el fin de semana), so 'this' is este.

a1-09.topic: Ir a + infinitive: the near future
a1-09.q: Complete: Mañana nosotros ___ cocinar una tortilla.
a1-09.why: Near future = ir + a + infinitive; with nosotros: vamos a cocinar.

a1-09.q: Complete: —¿___ vive tu familia? —Mi familia vive lejos.
a1-09.why: The answer 'lejos' (far away) gives a place, so the question word is ¿Dónde? (where), with an accent.

a1-09.q: What does 'Este sábado no va a estar sola' mean?
options: This Saturday she is not going to be alone.
Last Saturday she was not alone.
a1-09.why: 'Este sábado' = this Saturday, and 'no va a estar' = is not going to be.

a1-09.topic: Ir a + infinitive: the near future
a1-09.q: Javier talks about his plan. Complete: ___ a pasar el fin de semana aquí.
a1-09.why: For 'I am going to', use voy + a + infinitive: voy a pasar. 'Va' is he/she and 'vas' is you.

a1-10.q: Complete: ___ viernes ___ noche, los hermanos preparan las mochilas.
a1-10.why: No word for 'on' before days: el viernes. Without a clock time, use 'por la noche'; 'de la noche' only follows a clock time (a las diez de la noche).

a1-10.q: Complete: Elena se ríe y abre ___ bolsa. (her bag)
a1-10.why: Su means 'her' (and also 'his' or 'their'). Bolsa is singular, so su, not sus. Mi is 'my' and tu is 'your'.

a1-10.q: Complete: Raúl busca los billetes, pero no los ___. (find)
a1-10.why: Encontrar changes o → ue in the stressed stem: encuentra (he finds). 'Encontra' is not a form, 'encuentran' is they, and 'encontrar' is the infinitive.

a1-10.q: Elena asks Grandpa: '¿___ ir con nosotros?' (Do you want)
a1-10.why: Querer changes e → ie: quieres (you want). 'Quiere' is he/she and 'quiero' is I.

a1-10.q: How do you say 'The train leaves at eight in the morning'?
options: El tren sale a las ocho de la mañana.
El tren sale en las ocho de la mañana.
El tren sale las ocho de la mañana.
El tren sale a la ocho de la mañana.
a1-10.why: Clock time = 'a las + number', and after a clock time use 'de la mañana'.

a1-10.q: Grandpa says: «Es más grande que en ___ recuerdos.» (my memories)
a1-10.why: Recuerdos is plural, so mi becomes mis: possessives agree with the thing owned (many memories), not with the owner (one grandpa). Sus would mean his/their, and mío does not go before a noun.

a1-10.q: How do you say 'I want to see the sea'?
a1-10.why: With yo, querer becomes quiero (e → ie, ending -o). 'Quiere' is he/she, as in the story: el abuelo quiere ver el mar.

a1-10.q: Complete: Nosotros ___ ir a la playa. (want)
a1-10.why: With nosotros the stem does not change: queremos. 'Quieren' is they and 'quiere' is he/she.
